sections.html:
Otero County runs along the Texas line in south-central New Mexico, and Alamogordo is the county seat and only city. Cloudcroft and Tularosa are villages. Smaller places include Boles Acres, High Rolls, La Luz, Mayhill, Mescalero, Orogrande, Timberon and Holloman AFB. The 2020 census counted 67,839 people.

Holloman Air Force Base is the largest employer, followed by tourism around Cloudcroft, the Mescalero resort and White Sands National Park. Some owners are posted to the base for a set tour and leave on a fixed date, which can leave little time to manage repairs, a tax bill or a listing.

Two county offices share the work, and both sit at the same Alamogordo address. The Assessor finds, lists and values property. The Treasurer sends the bill and collects the money. If you disagree with a value, talk to the Assessor. If you want a payoff figure, ask the Treasurer.

OfficeWhat it doesAddress and phone
Otero County AssessorValues property, mails the notice of value, takes protests1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Alamogordo, NM 88310; 575-437-5310
Otero County TreasurerBills and collects property tax, takes payments1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310; 575-437-2030

Both county offices run searchable online records: the Treasurer's EagleWeb portal shows balances, and the Assessor's portal shows current ownership.

sections.h2: Due dates and how to pay
sections.html:
Otero County bills in two installments. The first half is due November 10 and goes delinquent after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and goes delinquent after May 10.

The Treasurer takes payment in person, by mail, online and by phone. The county's pay-by-phone page gives 1-877-707-1126, or 575-437-2030 and option 2. Card fees are 2.39 percent with a $1.95 minimum on a credit card and $3.95 on a debit card.

  • November 10: first half due
  • December 10: last day for the first half without penalty
  • April 10: second half due
  • May 10: last day for the second half without penalty

A bill you never received is still owed. New Mexico owners must pay whether or not the mail arrives, so keep your mailing address current with the Assessor.

The Assessor sets the value, and you have 30 days to contest it. Under Section 7-38-24 NMSA 1978, a petition goes to the county assessor by the later of April 1 or thirty days after the notice of valuation is mailed. It must name the owner and property, say why the value is wrong, and state what you believe the correct value is.

Each county has a valuation protests board of three voting members, and protests must be decided within 180 days of filing. If you disagree with the board, you can go to district court within thirty days of its order.

Home values for tax purposes are also capped. Section 7-36-21.2 limits a residential value to the higher of 103 percent of the prior year's value or 106.1 percent of the value two years earlier. The cap does not apply in the first year a property is valued, to improvements made in the prior year, or in a year after a change of ownership or a change of use or zoning.

That last exception matters if you plan to sell. A buyer can see a higher assessed value the year after closing, so your old bill is a poor guide to what the new owner will pay.

Unpaid tax first brings penalty and interest, and after enough years it can lead to a state auction. The Property Tax Division, not the county, holds these sales. The minimum bid is based on taxes, penalty, interest and costs, and sales happen where title research is done and other collection steps have run out. Not all 33 counties get an auction each year.

A tax sale clears the tax lien only; no other liens are extinguished. The state issues a tax deed that works like a quitclaim deed and does not warrant title. New Mexico has no right of redemption for former owners, though a two-year window under Section 7-38-70 lets someone challenge the sale in court.

If you own an Otero County house with several years of tax behind it, act early. Selling before the property reaches an auction list keeps the equity with you.

Most sellers need three things: a current payoff figure, a clean record of who owns the property, and a plan for the two installments. The Treasurer can supply the balance, and the title or escrow company will ask for it before closing.

  • Check the balance on the Treasurer's portal and confirm both halves of the current year.
  • Look for older years. Back tax that has been delinquent for years is the amount that can move a property toward auction.
  • Make sure the mailing address on file is current, because the notice of value and bill go to the address on the tax roll.
  • If the house is a mobile home, ask the Assessor about a tax release before you try to transfer the title.

Cash Home Buyers works with owners in this spot, including heirs who inherited a house with tax behind it and owners who left town. We buy as-is, so a stale tax bill, an unfinished repair or a tenant does not have to be solved first.

faqs.q: Where do I pay Otero County property tax?
faqs.a: The Otero County Treasurer is at 1104 N. White Sands Blvd., Suite A, Alamogordo, NM 88310, phone 575-437-2030. Payments can also be made online or by phone at 1-877-707-1126.

faqs.q: When is the first half of Otero County property tax due?
faqs.a: The first half is due November 10 and delinquent after December 10. The second half is due April 10 and delinquent after May 10.

faqs.q: How long do I have to protest my Otero County valuation?
faqs.a: You have until the later of April 1 or thirty days after the assessor mails the notice of valuation. File the petition with the Otero County Assessor, and state why you think the value is wrong and what you believe it should be.

faqs.q: Can the county sell my house at auction for unpaid tax?
faqs.a: The state, not the county, auctions property after long delinquency. The Property Tax Division sells it as is for at least the taxes, penalty, interest and costs, and New Mexico offers no right of redemption.

faqs.q: Can I sell an Otero County house that has tax due?
faqs.a: Yes. The balance is paid from the sale proceeds at closing, and a title company will request a payoff figure from the Treasurer. Selling before the property reaches an auction list avoids that outcome.
